build_inputs.angles:
1. Lead on this: 631 horsepower from 6.5 litres and twelve cylinders, with no turbochargers anywhere. Open on the engine and the cylinder count. Verify the figures against this exact car - the LP640 is not the earlier 6.2.
2. The core argument and the reason this video exists: this is an E-gear car, the automated manual, and that is why it sold for what it did. A factory gated manual LP640 is one of fewer than two hundred worldwide and asks several times the money - one has been listed close to two million dollars. Verify the production count and the premium independently, because sources disagree on both. The point is that on this car the gearbox is worth more than the car.
3. Then the modern twist, which is the hook for anybody who cares about three pedals: you can now buy a gated-manual conversion kit for a Murcielago for about forty thousand dollars. So the cheap automatic plus roughly forty grand gets you the gate and the click-clack. Be straight that a converted car is not a factory manual and collectors will not pay factory-manual money for one - the swap buys the experience, not the value.
4. Cover the catch, and the irony is the beat. The seller reported that a recent E-gear snap reading showed this car's clutch life was low and that it may need replacing soon, so a new clutch assembly was included with the sale. An E-gear clutch is one of the famous running costs on these - and in a gated manual conversion it is the first thing thrown away.
5. What the LP640 actually changed, in one beat: launched in 2007, displacement up to 6.5 litres for roughly sixty more horsepower, a revised clutch with launch control, more aggressive bumpers, LED tail lights and a single centre-exit exhaust.
6. Close on the question: would you take the cheap automatic and spend forty grand on a gate, or hold out for a factory manual at ten times the money?

script: 631 horsepower from 6.5 litres and twelve cylinders, without a single turbocharger to help shove air into the engine. That's the 2008 Lamborghini Murciélago LP640 Coupe; Lamborghini unveiled its replacement for the 6.2-litre version at Geneva in 2006 with increased bore and stroke. Its 487 lb-ft reaches all four wheels through six-speed E-gear, an automated manual rather than a conventional torque-converter automatic, with a revised clutch and launch control. Collectors want three pedals. Factory manual production is widely estimated below 200 worldwide, and factory cars can command about $900,000 for essentially the same engine. They go for about $460,000 today, while EAG sells a gated-manual conversion kit for about forty grand before installation. That includes hydraulic clutch hardware. Conversions don't buy factory provenance. You're buying the gate and the experience, not factory-manual collectibility. Would you convert this twelve-cylinder monster or pay the premium for an original?

sections.Highlights: THIS... is a 2008 Lamborghini Murciélago LP640 Coupe, finished in black with a black interior. The odometer on this Murciélago currently displays approximately 20,800 miles. The attached Carfax history report shows that this LP640 has been owned in Florida, Georgia, and California since new. Factory equipment includes 18-inch Hercules wheels, a front axle lift system, xenon headlights, LED tail lights, scissor doors, active rear air intakes, quilted leather upholstery with white contrast stitching, a Kenwood touchscreen head unit, and carbon fiber engine bay trim. Modifications reported by the seller include an aftermarket titanium exhaust system, an aftermarket rear spoiler, a hard-wired laser jammer/radar detector system, window tint, and paint protection film. Launched in 2007, the Murcielago LP640 received multiple updates with the most notable being the engine. Lamborghini increased the displacement of the V12 to 6.5-liters, which in turn gave the LP640 a near 60 horsepower bump. The E-Gear transmission received a revised clutch and a launch control setting. On the exterior, the LP640 was also given new, more aggressive front and rear bumpers, LED tail lights, and a single-exit exhaust. Power comes from a 6.5-liter V12 engine, rated at 631 horsepower and 487 lb-ft of torque. Output is sent to all four wheels via a 6-speed E-Gear automated manual transmission and a permanent all-wheel drive system.
